classification.difficultyReason: Apply a stated growth factor over successive decades and compare successive population values with a threshold.

questions.mappingNote: The whole question directly applies exponential growth. Part a evaluates accumulated growth factors; part b compares successive population values with a threshold without logarithms.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines positive whole-number powers as repeated multiplication. Page 3 explains products of powers. Question 1 supplies the factor of 3 per decade; evaluate successive powers and multiply the initial population by the corresponding factor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a stated growth factor over successive decades and compare successive population values with a threshold.

classification.difficultyReason: Generate powers by repeated multiplication, then select powers of related bases from a reference list.

questions.mappingNote: Part a evaluates successive powers of 2; b(i–iv) applies the same repeated-multiplication method to bases 3, 5, 6 and 7; c(i–ii) selects every second or third power of 2 to identify powers of 4 or 8.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines positive integer powers as repeated multiplication. Page 3 demonstrates multiplying indices for powers of powers. Question 2 supplies the zero-power starting value and requests successive reference lists.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generate powers by repeated multiplication, then select powers of related bases from a reference list.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct evaluation of numerical powers using positive, zero and negative indices.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and f evaluate positive powers; b–e apply powers of quotients; g applies the zero-index rule; h–o evaluate negative numerical powers. Negative-integer indices are the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Positive powers are repeated multiplication; powers of quotients raise numerator and denominator separately. Non-zero bases have zero power equal to one. Negative indices require taking the reciprocal first, then evaluating the positive power, as in Example 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct evaluation of numerical powers using positive, zero and negative indices.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly apply the supplied reciprocal reminder and evaluate small integer powers; one item uses the zero-index rule.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d take reciprocals of fractions; e–g take reciprocals of decimals; h evaluates a negative numerical power; i–n reciprocate before evaluating positive powers; o uses the zero-index rule. The primary skill is reciprocal-index-expressions.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 defines zero and negative indices. Page 5 explicitly requires taking the reciprocal first, writing a reciprocal fraction directly, then evaluating the positive power; Example 3 models this sequence. Question 4 repeats the reciprocal reminder.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly apply the supplied reciprocal reminder and evaluate small integer powers; one item uses the zero-index rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of product, quotient and power-of-a-power laws, including signed exponent arithmetic.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed skill is applying index laws with negative-integer indices. Parts a–h and q,t use products; i–p use quotients; r,s,u–x use powers of powers. Parts e,f,n also use the zero index.
questions.methodNote: Add indices for products, subtract divisor indices for quotients and multiply indices for powers of powers. These laws extend to zero and negative indices. Retain index form as explicitly requested in this question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of product, quotient and power-of-a-power laws, including signed exponent arithmetic.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the product and quotient power laws, raising every coefficient and variable to the given positive integer power.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c raise a coefficient and variable; d–e raise every factor in a product; f–h raise numerator and denominator; i–j combine both laws. All directly assess power-of-product-quotient.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 states the powers-of-products and powers-of-quotients laws. Page 4 Example 2 applies the power to every factor, including numerical coefficients, then evaluates numerical powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the product and quotient power laws, raising every coefficient and variable to the given positive integer power.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly apply the reciprocal rule, recognising the powered base and retaining external coefficients and signs; part h also applies the taught product-power law.

questions.mappingNote: All ten parts convert negative indices to fractions. Part h additionally squares both factors of the bracketed product; parts d, f, g, i and j distinguish external factors from the powered base.
questions.methodNote: Use a negative index to take the reciprocal first, as defined on PDF 4 and demonstrated in Example 3 on PDF 5. Apply the power to every factor inside brackets using PDF 3–4; retain coefficients and signs outside the powered base.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly apply the reciprocal rule, recognising the powered base and retaining external coefficients and signs; part h also applies the taught product-power law.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert mixed numerals and decimals to fractions, then take reciprocals and evaluate positive powers without a calculator.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess reciprocal powers of fractional bases, preceded by mixed-numeral or decimal conversion. The offered eight-part reuse candidate is not the same whole task.
questions.methodNote: Convert the base to a fraction as instructed, take its reciprocal first, then evaluate the positive power. Page 5 explicitly discourages compound reciprocal fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert mixed numerals and decimals to fractions, then take reciprocals and evaluate positive powers without a calculator.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine rectangular-prism volume, cubed metric conversion and division by the volume of one grain to estimate a very large count.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed step combines a cubed conversion factor with a large-number count, so calculations-scientific-notation is the closest catalogue match. Rectangular-prism volume and cubic-unit conversion support the calculation.
questions.methodNote: Use positive powers as repeated multiplication and the power-of-a-power law to cube the metric conversion factor. Calculate rectangular-prism volume in consistent units, then divide by the volume of one grain. The exercise instruction prohibits calculator use for question 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine rectangular-prism volume, cubed metric conversion and division by the volume of one grain to estimate a very large count.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly replace reciprocal variable powers with negative indices, retaining external signs and numerical coefficients.

questions.mappingNote: All ten parts directly assess conversion from fractions to negative-index expressions; numerical coefficients and external negative signs remain unchanged.
questions.methodNote: Use a^{-n}=1/a^n in reverse. Example 4 on PDF page 5 separates the coefficient from the reciprocal variable power before converting to a negative index.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly replace reciprocal variable powers with negative indices, retaining external signs and numerical coefficients.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise reciprocal powers, retain both square roots where the base is unknown, and equate linear indices after expressing both sides with a common base.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–h recognise powers directly; i–l solve for an unknown base using squares, cubes and reciprocals; m–p express both sides with a common base and equate indices. Pages 4–5 explicitly establish zero and negative powers, page 3 gives the power-of-a-power law, and page 6 supplies the exercise's no-calculator instruction.
questions.methodNote: Use the positive-power definition, power-of-a-power law, zero index and reciprocal interpretation of negative indices. Recognise equal powers without a calculator; for unknown bases undo the reciprocal and retain both signs for square roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise reciprocal powers, retain both square roots where the base is unknown, and equate linear indices after expressing both sides with a common base.

classification.difficultyReason: Select product, quotient and power laws, simplify algebraic exponents, and convert negative indices to reciprocal form.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–b use the product law; c combines algebraic exponents and a reciprocal; d uses the quotient law; e uses the power law; f combines the power law and a reciprocal; g combines power and product laws; h combines power and quotient laws.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 teaches adding indices for products, subtracting indices for quotients, and multiplying indices for powers of powers. Pages 4–5 define negative indices and Example 5 combines these laws before writing reciprocal answers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select product, quotient and power laws, simplify algebraic exponents, and convert negative indices to reciprocal form.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine coefficients and several variable powers, including negative powers of products and cancellation.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess these laws on multivariable terms; parts h, j and l also require powers of numerical coefficients. The exercise note prohibits calculators for Question 13.
questions.methodNote: Add indices for products, subtract indices for quotients and multiply indices for powers of powers. Raise every factor of a product, including its coefficient. Convert remaining negative powers to reciprocals, as in Example 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine coefficients and several variable powers, including negative powers of products and cancellation.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand three binomial squares, simplify the middle terms using index laws, and express negative powers as reciprocals.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess expansion and simplification of special products with negative indices. Page 6 supplies the exercise-wide no-calculator instruction; its single printed owner is outside this assignment.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 establishes product and power-of-a-power index laws; pages 4–5 define zero and negative indices and demonstrate simplification followed by reciprocal conversion. Expand each square using ordinary binomial multiplication, then apply these laws.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand three binomial squares, simplify the middle terms using index laws, and express negative powers as reciprocals.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied prime-factor demonstration, distribute variable exponents and collect exponents separately for each prime base.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded demonstration explicitly directs prime-base decomposition. Each of a–f assesses that method; e and f additionally combine negative indices. The inspected exercise note prohibits calculator use for Question 16.
questions.methodNote: Express composite bases as products of primes; apply powers of products, powers of powers, and product and quotient index laws, including negative indices.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied prime-factor demonstration, distribute variable exponents and collect exponents separately for each prime base.

classification.difficultyReason: Extend the supplied common-power factorisation to shifted exponents and quotients, including recognising the denominator as the remaining factor in f.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses factorisation of a sum or difference of powers; parts b, d and f additionally cancel common factors in a quotient. The embedded demonstration supplies the factorisation method beyond the earlier index-law examples.
questions.methodNote: Use product and quotient index laws, including negative indices, and the question's supplied demonstration of extracting a common power.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extend the supplied common-power factorisation to shifted exponents and quotients, including recognising the denominator as the remaining factor in f.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines rewriting composite-base powers, identifying common exponential factors and cancelling binomial factors, including a reversed subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess factorisation of exponential sums or differences after rewriting powers; common-prime-base manipulation supports the factorisation. The reference to earlier methods introduces no missing mathematical givens.
questions.methodNote: Apply the product, quotient and power-of-a-power laws. The embedded demonstrations in questions 16 and 17 show rewriting composite bases and taking out a common power before simplifying.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines rewriting composite-base powers, identifying common exponential factors and cancelling binomial factors, including a reversed subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate perfect powers by taking the indicated root before the numerator power; two parts first convert terminating decimal indices to fractions.

questions.mappingNote: All ten parts directly assess fractional indices. Parts a–c use unit fractional indices; d–h use a root followed by a whole-number power; i and j first express the decimal index as a fraction. The supplied substitution reuse candidate is a different complete task and is not reused.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines a unit fractional index as the corresponding non-negative root and Example 6 evaluates roots. Page 10 defines general fractional indices and Example 7 takes the denominator root before the numerator power. The question repeats that instruction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate perfect powers by taking the indicated root before the numerator power; two parts first convert terminating decimal indices to fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate fractional powers of fractions and decimals, converting decimal bases to fractions and taking the root before the power.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c evaluate unit fractional powers; d–e take a cube root before an integer power; f–h first convert decimal bases to fractions. All directly assess fractional indices. The supplied reuse candidate has different givens and tasks and is not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines fractional indices as roots. Page 10, General fractional indices and Example 7, demonstrates taking the denominator's root first and then the numerator's power, including fractional bases. Question 2 explicitly requires converting mixed numerals and decimals to fractions first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate fractional powers of fractions and decimals, converting decimal bases to fractions and taking the root before the power.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly stated reciprocal-first procedure, then take an exact root and integer power; the final items include fractional and mixed-number bases.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts evaluate negative fractional indices by the printed reciprocal-first method. Parts a–c and g–h require one root after inversion; d–f and i–l additionally require an integer power. Part k first converts the mixed numeral to 9/4. The fractional-indices skill directly covers the assessed root-and-power procedure; reciprocal-index-expressions records the inversion component. The supplied reuse candidate is a different complete substitution task and cannot be reused.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 defines fractional indices through non-negative roots. Page 10 Key Ideas 7–8 and Example 8 establish taking the reciprocal first, then the root indicated by the denominator, then the power indicated by the numerator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the explicitly stated reciprocal-first procedure, then take an exact root and integer power; the final items include fractional and mixed-number bases.

classification.difficultyReason: Select multiplication, division and power laws for fractional and negative indices, including multivariable terms and a powered coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b add indices; c combines coefficients and adds each variable's indices; d and e subtract indices; f divides coefficients and subtracts each variable's indices; g and h multiply indices; i distributes the power to every factor and evaluates the coefficient by taking its square root before cubing. Fractional indices is the closest catalogue skill for applying these laws to rational exponents.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select multiplication, division and power laws for fractional and negative indices, including multivariable terms and a powered coefficient.

classification.difficultyReason: Select product, quotient and power laws for fractional indices, then evaluate zero and negative powers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c add indices; d–f subtract indices; g combines multiplication and division; h–i multiply indices for a power of a power. Evaluate the resulting powers, using reciprocals for negative indices and 1 for a zero index.
questions.methodNote: Pages 9–10 extend the index laws to fractional indices, interpret roots and explain reciprocals for negative indices. Page 11 supplies the exercise-wide instruction to avoid calculators unless requested and presents the preceding index-law practice.
